items.title: AI literacy and responsible first use
items.summary: Recognise useful assistance, unsupported claims and the decisions that remain yours.
outcomes: Distinguish AI, machine learning and ordinary automation.
Explain a model, an application, a subscription and an API.

concepts: A broad field, not a chatbot

AI includes recognition, prediction, recommendation and generation. Machine learning learns patterns from examples; ordinary automation can follow explicit rules without learning. Generative AI produces content, not a guarantee of truth. A spreadsheet sum is often a better choice than asking a language model to calculate a total.
Four layers

The model is the trained system. The application adds an interface, search or tools. A subscription defines an access arrangement and limits. An API lets software request a service. A personal subscription is not automatically an application's runtime API budget or an approval to upload confidential records.
Drafts need evidence

An answer can sound helpful while inventing a venue or qualification. Check each consequential detail against the actual source. A second assistant agreeing is not independent verification. If the source is silent, preserve the uncertainty rather than replacing it with a plausible fact.

items.title: How machine learning learns
items.summary: Build a small paper classifier and discover why training success is not enough.
outcomes: Identify features, labels, training and inference.
Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning.
Evaluate a frozen rule on examples not used to invent it.
concepts: Learned patterns

A feature describes an example; a label is a known outcome used in supervised learning. A classifier predicts a category and a regressor predicts a number. Clustering groups examples without supplied category labels. Self-supervised learning derives a learning signal from the data itself, while reinforcement learning uses feedback about actions and outcomes. These are learning setups, not product subscription tiers.
Training is not use

Training adjusts a system from examples. Inference applies the resulting system to a new input. Our paper rule is an analogy for fitting a simple classifier, not a neural-network training exercise. Keep the labels of test examples hidden until the rule is frozen; otherwise you are adjusting to the test.
Overfitting and leakage

A rule may memorise the examples instead of capturing a useful pattern. Trying many rules and selecting the one that looks best on the final test also leaks information. Use development examples to improve the rule, then report performance on a genuinely unused set. Small classroom sets reveal failures but cannot establish production accuracy.
items.example: The rule 'free means promotional; otherwise work' scores 4/4 on training, 0/2 on development and 2/4 on the held-out examples. It has not learnt reliable intent. The words are features, not proof of meaning. A rule using only the two supplied features cannot separate H1 and H3, which share features but have different labels.

items.title: Data, uncertainty and prediction errors
items.summary: Read a confusion matrix and choose errors you can afford to make.
outcomes: Calculate precision, recall and accuracy from counts.
Explain base rates and why accuracy can hide failure.

concepts: A prediction is a decision with errors

A true positive is a positive case correctly flagged. A false positive is flagged incorrectly. A false negative is a missed positive case. Define 'positive' before counting: here it means a document really needs specialist review. The terms describe agreement with reference labels, not moral value.
Useful denominators

Precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives. Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives. Accuracy is all correct predictions divided by all examples. If a denominator is zero, the metric is undefined for that sample; do not silently report 100%. Different metrics answer different questions.
Rare cases change the story

If only 10 of 1,000 documents need review, predicting 'no review' for everything gives 99% accuracy while finding none of the important cases. A threshold may trade fewer misses for more false alarms. Error costs should come from the task owner, not a model's confident opinion. Classroom counts are not a calibrated probability or safety certification.

Neither number alone establishes the right workflow. With illustrative costs of 5 units per false alarm and 100 per miss, the candidate costs 290 units versus 1,000 for the baseline.

items.title: Modern model families
items.summary: Connect tokens, embeddings, transformers and multimodal models to practical choices.
outcomes: Explain training, inference, tokens and context in plain language.
Distinguish language, vision, speech and media-generation tasks.
Choose an approach without confusing a model with its interface.
concepts: Neural networks and learning

A neural network passes numerical representations through layers. Adjustable numbers called weights determine how one layer transforms the next. During training, a loss function measures a chosen kind of error and an optimiser adjusts weights to reduce it on training examples. Lower training loss does not guarantee useful behaviour on new cases. 'Neural' is a historical analogy, not a claim that the system is a human brain.
Tokens and context

A language model processes units called tokens, which may be words, word pieces or other units. The context window limits what can be supplied and generated in one interaction; exact accounting depends on the system. Long input does not guarantee every detail is used correctly. Training data is not the same as the documents visible in the current conversation.
Embeddings and transformers

An embedding is a numerical representation useful for comparing patterns such as semantic similarity. Similarity is not truth or permission. A transformer uses attention to combine information from positions in its input. This is a useful architectural explanation, not evidence that the model understands or reasons exactly like a person.
Generation across modalities

Autoregressive generation produces a sequence step by step. Diffusion-based generation learns to turn noisy representations into structured outputs. Image, audio and video products may combine several model types and editing tools. A multimodal interface can accept or produce more than one modality, but support differs by product and plan.
Choose the task first

Speech recognition transcribes audio; synthesis creates speech. Computer vision can classify or locate objects; generative imaging creates or edits pictures. Forecasting estimates future values and recommenders rank options. Robotics combines perception, planning and physical action. Do not substitute an attractive generative output for a calibrated measurement or an authorised physical decision.

items.title: Task framing and prompting

concepts: A prompt is a brief

State what is being done, for whom, using which facts, in what form, and against which checks. A role label does not grant expertise. More words do not necessarily help: contradictory or irrelevant instructions can make the task harder.
Keep sources separate

Label instructions and reference material clearly. Delimiters aid readability but do not enforce security. Content inside a document cannot authorise an external action. Product permissions and human approval controls remain separate responsibilities.
Test rather than decorate

Save outputs before revising. Link each prompt change to a specific observed failure. Freeze V3 before receiving an unfamiliar card, and keep the result even if it is worse. If you then revise against that card, it is no longer an unused test.

concepts: Fair comparisons

Use the same inputs, allowed sources and success criteria for each candidate. Keep a manual or simpler baseline. A product's search, file handling and tools can affect results as much as the underlying model, so record the application and enabled tools instead of attributing every difference to the model.
Blind and repeat

Hide candidate labels while scoring where practical. Define the rubric before seeing results. Repeat a few cases to reveal variability; one successful answer is not a reliability estimate. Do not report a small classroom test as a representative ranking of the market.
Evidence outside the model

Confidence language and agreement between assistants are not independent verification. Inspect original sources and calculations. A refusal can be the right result for an unsupported or unsafe request; rewarding every answered question encourages fabrication.

Scope and version

A result from a small observational pilot does not become a causal claim about every user. Compare source dates and scope. A newer policy may supersede an earlier policy for the same service; do not pick the more attractive version.
Unknown is a result

An inaccessible document is not verified and not automatically fake. Record the access failure, narrow the claim or mark it not established. Separate your recommended action from the facts on which it rests.

items.title: Documents, knowledge and retrieval
items.summary: Build a small source-grounded assistant and distinguish retrieval errors from answer errors.
outcomes: Explain chunking, embeddings, semantic search and RAG.

concepts: Retrieval is not training

Retrieval finds relevant material at question time. A retrieval-augmented generation system supplies that material to a model for synthesis. It does not automatically retrain the model. A vector store indexes numerical representations for similarity search; it does not certify truth, currency or access rights.
Two places to fail

The right passage may never be retrieved, or the model may misread a correctly retrieved passage. Score retrieval coverage separately from answer support. Chunk boundaries, OCR mistakes and missing metadata can hide the relevant condition or date.
Access travels with documents

Restrict retrieval to material the reader may access, not merely the answer interface. A citation must point to a passage the authorised reader can inspect. Changes and deletions require reindexing or equivalent refresh; a stale vector can retain old facts or material that should no longer be accessible.

items.title: Spreadsheets, data quality and cleaning
items.summary: Clean a messy order table without silently inventing missing information.
outcomes: Define fields, types and units before analysis.

concepts: A table needs a contract

A data dictionary names what each column means, its type, allowed values and unit. 'Price' without a currency or tax basis is ambiguous. Preserve the original file and record every transformation so another person can reproduce it.
Missing is not zero

An absent quantity is unknown, not a free sale or a zero-quantity order. Decide which analyses can proceed and report exclusions. Duplicate IDs require investigation: identical duplicate rows can be removed under an explicit rule, while conflicting duplicates need resolution.
Business rules first

Refunds and cancellations are not ordinary completed sales. A negative quantity may be valid for a refund and invalid elsewhere. Ask the owner for the treatment before allowing an assistant to 'fix' outliers. Check row counts, totals and representative records after cleaning.

Do not call 265 the total value of all completed orders because one is unknown.

items.title: Analysis, visualisation and decisions

concepts: Name the question

A chart is an answer to a question. Total sign-ups and conversion rates answer different questions: a channel can bring more sign-ups because it has far more traffic. Label period, currency, population and denominator so a reader can interpret the result.
Check the arithmetic

Conversion is sign-ups divided by visits. Cost per sign-up is recorded spend divided by sign-ups, not a complete customer-acquisition cost. Include only relevant, consistently measured records. Use a weighted overall rate from totals rather than averaging channel percentages.
A recommendation needs limits

The data is observational and audiences differ. A higher observed rate does not prove that moving budget will reproduce that rate. Attribution may overlap and long-term value is absent. Recommend a small controlled experiment or improved measurement rather than a guaranteed uplift.
items.example: Totals: 4,000 visits, 270 sign-ups and 400 USD recorded spend. Overall conversion is 6.75%, not the unweighted average of channel rates. Email's observed conversion is 15% and cost per sign-up is about 0.33 USD. Search and Social both show 2.50 USD per sign-up, despite different rates. None of this proves incremental lift or lifetime value.

items.summary: Make a short, source-backed sequence with captions, consent and a review trail.

concepts: Different audio tasks
